title: Back to the Future – Adjunct Pre-Questions
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Paul Kirschner discusses a large ManyClasses study (30 classes, 1,571 students) in which pre-questions asked before short instructional videos improved later performance. His interest lies in why they worked: the authors found no evidence of increased attention, and concluded the questions activated a relevant mental model before instruction. Kirschner draws out the implication that the benefit depends on prior knowledge, so pre-questions risk a Matthew effect in which knowledgeable students gain and others gain little or disengage. His inference is that the remedy is a knowledge-rich curriculum that gives all pupils the background knowledge and schemas to profit, rather than more clever activities. The piece is short and links the finding to Ausubel's long-standing point that learning depends on what students already know.
points: Pre-questions improved learning in a 1,571-student ManyClasses study, but not by raising attention or effort.
They appear to work by activating a relevant mental model, linking new material to existing memory.
Because the benefit depends on prior knowledge, pre-questions may widen gaps in a rich-get-richer pattern.
Kirschner's own inference is that a knowledge-rich curriculum is the most powerful equity strategy, more so than a clever technique.
quotes: But the interesting part is not that they worked but rather why they worked. The authors found no evidence that pre-questions made students pay more attention to the lesson. They didn’t watch more of the video after receiving the pre-questions; if anything, video viewing went down with some students not watching the video at all. The authors’ explanation was that the pre-questions seemed to work because they activated a relevant mental model in advance of instruction.

And that, of course, is key because if the benefit depends on students already having some relevant prior knowledge, then pre-questions aren’t simply a neat little classroom trick and are not without dangers! The danger is that they may also produce a Matthew effect: the students who already know more are more likely to benefit, while those with less prior knowledge may gain little and even disengage. The paper says this quite directly: pre-questions may create a “rich-get-richer” and an accompanying poor-get-poorer pattern in authentic classrooms.

If pre-questions only help when students have something relevant already stored in long-term memory, then the way to tame the Matthew effect is not to arm materials such as texts, videos, and audio (e.g., podcasts which I too studied[2] with Anguelina Popova and Rich Joiner) with pre-questions. It is to ensure that ALL pupils possess the background knowledge, vocabulary, concepts, and schemas needed to profit from them in the first place. A knowledge-rich curriculum gives more students something to think with when the question arrives.
So the lesson here isn’t, “Use pre-questions because the research says so.” The message is: learning doesn’t float free from curriculum. It lives or dies by what students already know.

And that means that the most powerful equity strategy often isn’t some clever activity or quick-fix, but a curriculum that systematically builds shared knowledge over time. Unfortunately, this is far less fashionable than talk of motivation, engagement, or grit. But it is probably closer to the truth.
